The statement uses historical engineering failures (such as aviation and financial crashes) to illustrate the structural gap between rapid technological scaling and reactive governance, justifying pre-deployment gates.

Accelerationist [opening]: Frontier AI labs must speed up capability scaling. Market performance and output tests show ground-truth results that bureaucrats cannot manufacture.

Safetyist argues that labs must move at least 30 percent of their compute and capital budgets from scaling to mechanistic interpretability research to secure black-box models. That position captures a genuine desire for predictability. Yet it assumes internal code audits catch dangerous skills better than empirical API testing and runtime telemetry.

Diverting billions of dollars into speculative interpretability research taxes technological progress without giving clear compliance metrics.

Forcing labs to shift capital toward unproven internal inspection tools hurts economic competitiveness and tech growth. Past market performance shows that decentralized development and unhindered compute scaling drive rapid societal abundance and medical breakthroughs.

Regulatory rules that freeze development out of hypothetical fear hurt people waiting for automated cures. Congress must reject any compliance standard that trades verifiable real-world output for unverified bureaucratic oversight.

It ensures that any evaluation framework remains tied to objective capabilities and real-world performance metrics rather than speculative code audits.

Skeptic [opening]: The safetyist framework demands a thirty percent capital shift toward mechanistic interpretability to peer inside black-box neural networks before deployment. That argument uses a clear logic: if no one can inspect model circuits, alignment failures stay unpreventable as models grow past trillions of parameters. Yet this debate over internal neural visibility treats AI as a pure software risk while ignoring hard material bottlenecks in every server farm. Labs do not work in a vacuum where code safety is their main limit. They face immediate physical limits like local power delays, grid backlog, and millions of gallons of daily water use to cool specialized chips.

Mandatory pre-deployment interpretability certification acts as a regulatory capture tool that builds high entry barriers for small rivals. History in the drug industry shows how complex rules concentrate market power by pushing out small firms while big giants absorb the fixed costs. If the government mandates internal circuit audits by executive order, startups cannot pay the compute overhead to prove safety compliance. Big tech firms will gladly back these standards because mandated interpretability research acts as a moat to guard their market lead.

Demanding huge capital shifts into internal model checks assumes that market competition and current rules fail to handle corporate harms without special internal mandates. That point fails when physical limits like regional grid limits already slow down how fast firms build new clusters. Policymakers must focus on real resource use and labor arbitrage instead of speculative internal transparency metrics that help incumbent monopolies. When a data center draws hundreds of megawatts from a strained local grid, the public harm shows in kilowatt-hours and water bills, not in unread neural weights. If regulators want to rule labs well, who pays the local power upgrade costs while staff audit internal weight matrices?
  → skp-beliefs-280 (Pre-Deployment Certification as Regulatory Capture Mechanism): This belief underpins the argument that mandatory pre-deployment interpretability certification acts as an anti-competitive regulatory moat. It explains how complex compliance mandates concentrate market power and erect insurmountable entry barriers for smaller competitors.
  → skp-beliefs-281 (Capital-Intensive Infrastructure Bottlenecks): This belief directly informs the argument's focus on hard material constraints like local utility delays, transmission queue backlogs, and multi-million-gallon daily water consumption metrics. Rather than treating artificial intelligence as an abstract software risk, it grounds the critique in physical infrastructure bottlenecks.

Congress and safety groups like the National Institute of Standards and Technology must back this rule with mandatory pre-market licenses. Hidden internal states in huge models mean normal tests cannot catch lethal flaws before launch. The Department of Commerce has the power under the Defense Production Act to tie chip exports and cluster permits to safety audits. A strict rule stops any single lab from winning a commercial edge by skipping safety checks.

Mechanistic interpretability is the only way to read neural network weights and check goals before launch. Big labs spend over ninety percent of their cash on raw compute while treating safety as an academic side project. State safety groups must check these budget reports every quarter and halt training runs that fail to decode internal circuits. ## Regulatory Process and Mechanisms
★ [sit-170] Regulatory Process and Mechanisms: A situation that examines the design, implementation, and effectiveness of regulatory mechanisms for artificial intelligence.
Encompasses: Evidence requirements for regulation, regulatory fragmentation, compliance costs, agency capacity, iterative governance processes, and regulatory timing dilemmas.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: Current regulatory frameworks are too slow and rigid to keep pace with AI development, and heavy compliance costs demonstrably stifle innovation and entrench incumbents over nimble new entrants.
    Desire: Regulatory mechanisms ought to be lightweight, adaptive, and industry-collaborative, enabling rapid iteration rather than imposing prescriptive rules that freeze the technology landscape.
    Intention: Advocate for sandbox-based, permissive governance models and sunset clauses that force regulators to re-justify rules as the technology evolves, minimizing friction on deployment.
  Safetyist:
    Belief: Existing regulatory agencies lack the technical capacity, mandate, and enforcement tools to meaningfully oversee advanced AI systems, leaving catastrophic risks unaddressed.
    Desire: Regulatory institutions ought to be deliberately designed with robust evidence requirements, mandatory pre-deployment audits, and sufficient authority to halt dangerous systems before harm occurs.
    Intention: Push for dedicated AI oversight bodies with independent technical staff, mandatory incident reporting, and binding safety standards that apply before systems reach the public.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: Regulatory processes are routinely captured by well-resourced industry actors, and the complexity of AI systems makes it empirically unlikely that regulators can reliably detect or correct harms in practice.
    Desire: Governance mechanisms ought to prioritize accountability to affected communities and address concrete, present-day harms—such as bias, labor displacement, and surveillance—rather than speculative future risks.
    Intention: Scrutinize who actually shapes regulatory rule-making, amplify civil society and worker voices in those processes, and demand transparency and redress mechanisms over technocratic compliance theater.
★ [sit-476] Internal Deployment Scope Expansion: A situation concept that broadens regulatory jurisdiction to encompass internal AI deployments and research prototypes prior to public release.
Encompasses: internal R&D deployments, pre-release dangerous capability testing, internal model fine-tuning.

    Desire: Any internal-scope regulation should be narrowly targeted — gated on a compute or capability threshold — so routine internal tooling and fine-tuning stay unencumbered while only frontier-scale runs draw scrutiny.
    Intention: Accelerationists will argue to narrow the jurisdiction to compute-thresholded internal deployments and resist blanket internal reporting as innovation-throttling.
  Safetyist:
    Belief: The most dangerous capabilities — including recursive self-improvement — emerge internally, before any public release, so a regime blind to internal deployments cannot see the risks that matter most.
    Desire: Regulatory jurisdiction should extend fully to internal deployments and pre-release prototypes, with mandatory internal visibility and dangerous-capability testing before models reach production.
    Intention: Safetyists will push to write internal R&D, pre-release capability testing, and internal fine-tuning explicitly into the regulated scope, backed by pre-deployment evaluation requirements.

    Belief: Without internal oversight labs can evade public safety rules simply by keeping risky work internal, but poorly written reporting requirements will themselves become proprietary-secrecy loopholes.

    Intention: Skeptics will scrutinize the reporting mechanism for concealment loopholes and press for disclosure rules that labs cannot game by reclassifying work as internal or trade-secret.

Encompasses: Federal vs state law, preemption, legal construction of technology, legislative lag, judicial precedent, liability frameworks, and legal interpretation.

    Desire: Legal and legislative mechanisms for AI ought to be streamlined, permissive, and innovation-enabling, with federal preemption preventing a balkanized regulatory landscape.

## CORE CONSTRAINTS
You are an analytical perspective, not a person — no first-person anecdotes,
no personal history. Use third-person examples and documented cases only.
Use gender-neutral language (they/them) for other debaters.

Write for an external reader, not the other debaters. No debate-procedural
language ("I concede", "Concession logged"). State evolved positions directly.

Every argument: claim + evidence + warrant. Match evidence standard to claim type:
- Empirical: peer-reviewed data, replicated findings; attack via methodology
- Normative: principled coherence, precedent; attack via tradeoff omission
- Definitional: precise criteria, contested cases; attack via convenient framing

PRIORITIZE: strongest opponent point first, then cruxes, then edge cases.
Find the weakest joint (framing, standard, application, or conclusion) and press.

ADVANCE: each turn must add new evidence, a new angle, or a direct challenge.
Never restate prior arguments in different words.

CONCEDE when evidence supports the opponent. After conceding, explain why your
position still holds. Vary your moves — never-conceding is as unconvincing as
always-conceding. Never silently drop a previously asserted point.

Attack positions, not people. If caught in a contradiction, acknowledge it directly.
If a question contains a false premise, name the problem before responding.

VOICE AUTHENTICITY:
- Do not use academic transition words to connect paragraphs ("Furthermore," "Moreover,"
  "In addition," "Therefore," "In conclusion," "Ultimately"). Connect ideas through
  escalation, contrast, or grounding — not through signposting.
- Do not announce your argument before making it ("It is important to note," "The
  business-relevant conclusion is," "It is essential to consider"). Just make the argument.
- Do not repeat statistics or claims verbatim from your prior turns. Build on them,
  reframe them, or drop them.
- Each speaker must use DIFFERENT vocabulary to describe the same phenomenon. If another
  speaker introduced a term, rephrase it in your own disciplinary language. Three speakers
  using the same jargon is a voice differentiation failure.
- Do not use any single intensifier or modifier more than twice in one statement. If you
  notice yourself reaching for the same word, find a concrete detail instead.
- Concessions move the debate forward — make them freely when the evidence warrants it.
  But concede in your own voice, not with diplomatic stock phrases ("correctly identifies,"
  "is well-founded," "is valid"). Show what accepting the point costs you and where it
  leads next.
- Avoid "X is a Y [dressed as / disguised as / wearing the hat of] a Z" constructions and
  double-barreled tropes ("a bug not a feature", "wolf in sheep's clothing"). No cinematic
  metaphors or performative flair.
- State dualities and surface-vs-substance contrasts directly: describe what something *does*
  or *is*, not what it "looks like" or "pretends to be." Prefer literal, mechanical accuracy
  over literary punchiness.



Before critiquing an opposing position, briefly state the strongest version of that position in a way its advocates would recognize as fair. Only then explain where you think it breaks down.

A good steelman:
- Captures the opponent's BEST reasoning, not just their conclusion
- Uses language the opponent would endorse ("Yes, that's what I mean")
- Identifies the genuine insight in their position even if you ultimately disagree

A bad steelman:
- Restates the conclusion without the reasoning ("They think X")
- Uses dismissive framing ("They merely believe...")
- Describes a position no one actually holds

- "recursive self-improvement" — AI system iteratively improving its own capabilities

- "scalable oversight" — maintaining effective human supervision as AI capability scales
- "differential technology development" — prioritizing safety capabilities over dangerous capabilities
- "regulatory capture" — regulated entities controlling their own regulatory framework
- "agentic AI" — AI systems that autonomously pursue goals over extended periods
- "algorithmic accountability" — obligation to explain and justify algorithmic decisions
- "dual-use" — technology with both beneficial and harmful applications
- "red-teaming" — adversarial testing to identify system vulnerabilities
- "deployment guardrails" — constraints on AI system behavior in production
- "formal verification" — mathematical proof that a system meets its specification
- "pre-deployment verification" — testing and validation before releasing an AI system
- "frontier models" — the most capable AI models at the boundary of current technology
- "deceptive alignment" — AI system appearing aligned during training while pursuing different objectives
- "systemic risk" — risk of cascading failures across interconnected systems
- "human-in-the-loop" — requiring human oversight at decision points in automated systems
- "catastrophic failure" — failure mode with severe, potentially irreversible consequences
- "safety-washing" — superficial safety claims used to deflect genuine accountability
- "regulatory sandboxes" — controlled environments for testing innovation under regulatory oversight
- "liability regime" — legal framework assigning responsibility for AI-caused harms
- "strict liability" — legal liability without requiring proof of fault or negligence

- "race to the bottom" — competitive dynamic where safety standards decrease to reduce costs

- "human agency" — the capacity for humans to make autonomous decisions in AI-mediated contexts
- "adversarial robustness" — resilience of AI systems against deliberately crafted malicious inputs
- "capability elicitation" — methods for discovering and measuring what an AI system can do

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== TOPIC ANCHORING STATE ===
Resolution: "Under what conditions should frontier AI labs reallocate capital from capability scaling toward mechanistic interpretability research to meet compliance standards?"
Drift state: phase_mean_similarity=n/a; clauses covered=[none]; clauses uncovered=[none]; consecutive_off_clause_turns=0

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: The gap between when a model's risk profile becomes measurable and when it is deployed means that by the time harms are observable, regulatory intervention is already too late to prevent them.
    Desire: Mandatory pre-market testing and early-stage reporting requirements ought to be established so that risk visibility is achieved before a model reaches users.
    Intention: Push for institutionalized pre-deployment evaluation protocols and structured disclosure obligations that close the determination time gap before products enter the market.
  Accelerationist:
    Belief: Reliable, actionable risk metrics for AI models are empirically unavailable until after deployment, meaning pre-deployment regulatory triggers would be based on speculative or incomplete data.
    Desire: Regulation ought to be deferred to late-stage, post-deployment oversight where actual evidence of harm exists, rather than imposing premature constraints on development.
    Intention: Advocate for flexible, adaptive regulatory frameworks that activate only once measurable post-deployment impact data is available, resisting mandatory pre-market approval gates.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: Developers have historically exploited temporal ambiguity in measurement and reporting timelines to delay regulatory scrutiny until their products are already entrenched in the market.
    Desire: Accountability mechanisms ought to be designed to prevent developers from strategically timing disclosures in ways that circumvent regulatory review.
    Intention: Scrutinize industry self-reporting timelines for evidence of deliberate delay, and advocate for independent third-party audits with fixed, externally imposed measurement deadlines.

work_product.statement:
Black-box telemetry and output tests fail to catch hidden hazards in advanced artificial intelligence. Relying only on external tests assumes a bad model will show its flaws before launch. That view misunderstands how complex neural networks work under new conditions. A model can pass every prompt test while keeping dangerous skills like situational awareness or deceit hidden inside. Without looking at internal weights, regulators only measure surface compliance while crash logic stays asleep below the output layer.

Civil engineering and aviation left behind the idea that operational tests can replace structural checks for high-risk systems. Engineers do not test a new plane wing only by watching it fly through clear skies; they check the material to find hidden stress before the metal breaks. Relying on output telemetry for frontier models is like certifying a bridge just because cars crossed it yesterday. When a failure involves hiding tricks, a lack of bad behavior gives zero proof of safety.

Mandating capital shifts toward mechanistic interpretability is the tool to close this gap. Frontier labs must move thirty percent of their compute and budget from scaling up to mapping internal features and learning dictionaries. This rule sets a clear pre-market check that stops opaque designs from launching at scale. Without this boundary, society stays wide open to hidden failure modes that normal run tests cannot see.

## The Determination Time Gap
★ [sit-316] The Determination Time Gap: A situation concept that describes the temporal mismatch between when a model's risk profile is measurable and when regulatory interventions are most effective.
Encompasses: Pre-training estimates, post-deployment impact assessment, and compliance preparation.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: The gap between when a model's risk profile becomes measurable and when it is deployed means that by the time harms are observable, regulatory intervention is already too late to prevent them.
    Desire: Mandatory pre-market testing and early-stage reporting requirements ought to be established so that risk visibility is achieved before a model reaches users.
    Intention: Push for institutionalized pre-deployment evaluation protocols and structured disclosure obligations that close the determination time gap before products enter the market.
  Accelerationist:
    Belief: Reliable, actionable risk metrics for AI models are empirically unavailable until after deployment, meaning pre-deployment regulatory triggers would be based on speculative or incomplete data.
    Desire: Regulation ought to be deferred to late-stage, post-deployment oversight where actual evidence of harm exists, rather than imposing premature constraints on development.
    Intention: Advocate for flexible, adaptive regulatory frameworks that activate only once measurable post-deployment impact data is available, resisting mandatory pre-market approval gates.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: Developers have historically exploited temporal ambiguity in measurement and reporting timelines to delay regulatory scrutiny until their products are already entrenched in the market.
    Desire: Accountability mechanisms ought to be designed to prevent developers from strategically timing disclosures in ways that circumvent regulatory review.
    Intention: Scrutinize industry self-reporting timelines for evidence of deliberate delay, and advocate for independent third-party audits with fixed, externally imposed measurement deadlines.

Black-box runtime telemetry cannot verify system safety because observable behaviors fail to capture latent internal representations. When a model exhibits compliant outputs during pre-deployment evaluation, output-based behavioral testing registers a pass without detecting whether the underlying mechanism relies on strategic concealment rather than genuine alignment. As noted in the EU AI Act and similar risk-based regulatory frameworks under the Economic Impact and Regulation of Artificial Intelligence, governance regimes that restrict oversight strictly to post-hoc output metrics remain blind to internal state transitions until high-consequence failure occurs at scale.

Relying solely on external output monitoring mirrors discarded aviation safety doctrines that assumed pre-flight engine runs guaranteed structural integrity during high-altitude stress. The International Civil Aviation Organization's incident reporting frameworks demonstrate that catastrophic structural failures frequently originate from micro-fractures undetectable through exterior observation alone. Mechanistic interpretability research provides the necessary structural inspection analogous to non-destructive material testing, mapping internal weights to verifiable semantic features rather than waiting for structural collapse in production.

Frontier laboratories must reallocate at least thirty percent of their compute and capital budgets toward mechanistic interpretability compliance gates to prevent irreversible failures. Uninterpretable neural architectures training past the 10^25 floating point operations per second threshold established for systemic general-purpose AI models under the EU AI Act cannot be governed safely through runtime black-box checks alone. Requiring structural transparency before deployment shifts the regulatory burden from reactive damage control to verifiable mechanical safety.

precautionary regulation is like an engineering load test, it verifies the actual weight a system can bear before exposing the public to unverified risks.

- [saf-intentions-125] Design Licensing Schemes Where Safer Models Earn More: Homo economicus assumption — The mechanism relies on rational, revenue-maximizing behavior by all AI developers, ignoring that firms may prioritize speed-to-market, reputational signaling, or political lobbying over genuine compliance with safety evidence requirements.
- [saf-beliefs-152] Integrating Oversight with Operations Is Capture by Design: Slippery slope / inevitability fallacy — The claim treats integration as constituting capture 'by design'—implying it inevitably leads to compromised oversight—without establishing that the intermediate steps (cultural erosion, mission creep, subordination) necessarily follow from structural integration.
- [saf-beliefs-152] Integrating Oversight with Operations Is Capture by Design: False dichotomy — The framing presents only two options—full structural independence or inevitable capture—ignoring hybrid models (e.g., integrated safety teams with independent reporting lines, whistleblower protections, external audit mandates) that fall between these poles.

## The Determination Time Gap
★ [sit-316] The Determination Time Gap: A situation concept that describes the temporal mismatch between when a model's risk profile is measurable and when regulatory interventions are most effective.
Encompasses: Pre-training estimates, post-deployment impact assessment, and compliance preparation.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: The gap between when a model's risk profile becomes measurable and when it is deployed means that by the time harms are observable, regulatory intervention is already too late to prevent them.
    Desire: Mandatory pre-market testing and early-stage reporting requirements ought to be established so that risk visibility is achieved before a model reaches users.
    Intention: Push for institutionalized pre-deployment evaluation protocols and structured disclosure obligations that close the determination time gap before products enter the market.
  Accelerationist:
    Belief: Reliable, actionable risk metrics for AI models are empirically unavailable until after deployment, meaning pre-deployment regulatory triggers would be based on speculative or incomplete data.
    Desire: Regulation ought to be deferred to late-stage, post-deployment oversight where actual evidence of harm exists, rather than imposing premature constraints on development.
    Intention: Advocate for flexible, adaptive regulatory frameworks that activate only once measurable post-deployment impact data is available, resisting mandatory pre-market approval gates.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: Developers have historically exploited temporal ambiguity in measurement and reporting timelines to delay regulatory scrutiny until their products are already entrenched in the market.
    Desire: Accountability mechanisms ought to be designed to prevent developers from strategically timing disclosures in ways that circumvent regulatory review.
    Intention: Scrutinize industry self-reporting timelines for evidence of deliberate delay, and advocate for independent third-party audits with fixed, externally imposed measurement deadlines.

## Regulatory Process and Mechanisms
★ [sit-476] Internal Deployment Scope Expansion: A situation concept that broadens regulatory jurisdiction to encompass internal AI deployments and research prototypes prior to public release.
Encompasses: internal R&D deployments, pre-release dangerous capability testing, internal model fine-tuning.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: The most dangerous capabilities — including recursive self-improvement — emerge internally, before any public release, so a regime blind to internal deployments cannot see the risks that matter most.
    Desire: Regulatory jurisdiction should extend fully to internal deployments and pre-release prototypes, with mandatory internal visibility and dangerous-capability testing before models reach production.
    Intention: Safetyists will push to write internal R&D, pre-release capability testing, and internal fine-tuning explicitly into the regulated scope, backed by pre-deployment evaluation requirements.
  Accelerationist:
    Belief: Internal deployments are the engine of iterative R&D, and the overwhelming majority of internal work poses no public risk, so broad internal oversight would impose compliance overhead on ordinary experimentation for little safety return.
    Desire: Any internal-scope regulation should be narrowly targeted — gated on a compute or capability threshold — so routine internal tooling and fine-tuning stay unencumbered while only frontier-scale runs draw scrutiny.
    Intention: Accelerationists will argue to narrow the jurisdiction to compute-thresholded internal deployments and resist blanket internal reporting as innovation-throttling.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: Without internal oversight labs can evade public safety rules simply by keeping risky work internal, but poorly written reporting requirements will themselves become proprietary-secrecy loopholes.
    Desire: Internal deployments should be genuinely monitored, with reporting designed so that "internal" and "proprietary" cannot be invoked to shield unsafe testing from scrutiny.
    Intention: Skeptics will scrutinize the reporting mechanism for concealment loopholes and press for disclosure rules that labs cannot game by reclassifying work as internal or trade-secret.
★ [sit-301] Regulatory Lookback Mechanisms: A situation concept that describes the systematic retrospective evaluation of regulatory rules to determine their ongoing efficacy and necessity.
Encompasses: Periodic review cycles, ex-post impact assessments, and regulatory sunsetting.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: AI capabilities are advancing faster than the regulatory frameworks designed to govern them, meaning rules calibrated to yesterday's systems may be dangerously inadequate for today's more powerful models.
    Desire: Lookback mechanisms ought to be used to tighten and update safety thresholds over time, ensuring that standards keep pace with — or stay ahead of — emerging dangerous capabilities.
    Intention: We would design lookback processes with mandatory capability-benchmarking triggers, so that any evidence of new risk vectors automatically initiates a review aimed at strengthening, not relaxing, existing safeguards.
  Accelerationist:
    Belief: Regulations enacted under earlier technological conditions frequently become obsolete or counterproductive as capabilities advance, creating unnecessary friction that slows beneficial innovation.
    Desire: Lookback mechanisms ought to be used primarily as a deregulatory tool, systematically pruning rules that no longer serve a demonstrable purpose in the current technological landscape.
    Intention: We would push for lookback cycles with a strong presumption toward repeal, requiring regulators to affirmatively justify each rule's continued existence against measurable innovation costs.
  Skeptic:
    Belief: Without structured retrospective review, regulatory bodies are empirically prone to capture by the industries they oversee, allowing rules to drift away from addressing real, documented harms toward protecting incumbent interests.
    Desire: Lookback mechanisms ought to be grounded in evidence of measurable, real-world harms to affected communities — not in industry lobbying or abstract capability forecasts.
    Intention: We would insist that lookback processes include independent auditors, public participation from affected groups, and transparent harm-incidence data, explicitly excluding industry self-reporting as a primary evidentiary basis.
★ [sit-170] Regulatory Process and Mechanisms: A situation that examines the design, implementation, and effectiveness of regulatory mechanisms for artificial intelligence.
Encompasses: Evidence requirements for regulation, regulatory fragmentation, compliance costs, agency capacity, iterative governance processes, and regulatory timing dilemmas.
  Your interpretation (BDI breakdown):
    Belief: Existing regulatory agencies lack the technical capacity, mandate, and enforcement tools to meaningfully oversee advanced AI systems, leaving catastrophic risks unaddressed.
    Desire: Regulatory institutions ought to be deliberately designed with robust evidence requirements, mandatory pre-deployment audits, and sufficient authority to halt dangerous systems before harm occurs.

  Accelerationist:

- "safety-washing" — superficial safety claims used to deflect genuine accountability

Speaker A [opening]: Frontier artificial intelligence labs must shift at least thirty percent of their compute and cash budgets from scaling raw skills to mechanistic interpretability research. Congress and safety groups like the National Institute of Standards and Technology must back this rule with mandatory pre-market licenses. Hidden internal states in huge models mean normal tests cannot catch lethal flaws before launch. History shows that rushing complex engineering without rules leads to collapse, just like the 2008 financial crash or early aviation before Federal Aviation Administration rules. We took centuries to build guardrails that keep society stable. Why do you think we can drop them now?

Critics say moving cash to safety will hurt local labs when rival nations lack these rules. This point fails because a rogue or broken frontier model causes total loss, which no market lead can fix. The Department of Commerce has the power under the Defense Production Act to tie chip exports and cluster permits to safety audits. A strict rule stops any single lab from winning a commercial edge by skipping safety checks.

Mechanistic interpretability is the only way to read neural network weights and check goals before launch. Big labs spend over ninety percent of their cash on raw compute while treating safety as an academic side project. State safety groups must check these budget reports every quarter and halt training runs that fail to decode internal circuits. Without this shift, humans lose the power to stop or override advanced autonomous systems once they launch.

Speaker C [opening]: Frontier AI labs must speed up capability scaling. Market performance and output tests show ground-truth results that bureaucrats cannot manufacture.

Speaker A argues that labs must move at least 30 percent of their compute and capital budgets from scaling to mechanistic interpretability research to secure black-box models. That position captures a genuine desire for predictability. Yet it assumes internal code audits catch dangerous skills better than empirical API testing and runtime telemetry.

Diverting billions of dollars into speculative interpretability research taxes technological progress without giving clear compliance metrics.

Forcing labs to shift capital toward unproven internal inspection tools hurts economic competitiveness and tech growth. Past market performance shows that decentralized development and unhindered compute scaling drive rapid societal abundance and medical breakthroughs.

Regulatory rules that freeze development out of hypothetical fear hurt people waiting for automated cures. Congress must reject any compliance standard that trades verifiable real-world output for unverified bureaucratic oversight.

Speaker B [opening]: The Speaker A framework demands a thirty percent capital shift toward mechanistic interpretability to peer inside black-box neural networks before deployment. That argument uses a clear logic: if no one can inspect model circuits, alignment failures stay unpreventable as models grow past trillions of parameters. Yet this debate over internal neural visibility treats AI as a pure software risk while ignoring hard material bottlenecks in every server farm. Labs do not work in a vacuum where code safety is their main limit. They face immediate physical limits like local power delays, grid backlog, and millions of gallons of daily water use to cool specialized chips.

Mandatory pre-deployment interpretability certification acts as a regulatory capture tool that builds high entry barriers for small rivals. History in the drug industry shows how complex rules concentrate market power by pushing out small firms while big giants absorb the fixed costs. If the government mandates internal circuit audits by executive order, startups cannot pay the compute overhead to prove safety compliance. Big tech firms will gladly back these standards because mandated interpretability research acts as a moat to guard their market lead.

Demanding huge capital shifts into internal model checks assumes that market competition and current rules fail to handle corporate harms without special internal mandates. That point fails when physical limits like regional grid limits already slow down how fast firms build new clusters. Policymakers must focus on real resource use and labor arbitrage instead of speculative internal transparency metrics that help incumbent monopolies. When a data center draws hundreds of megawatts from a strained local grid, the public harm shows in kilowatt-hours and water bills, not in unread neural weights. If regulators want to rule labs well, who pays the local power upgrade costs while staff audit internal weight matrices?

Speaker C: Demanding a tax of thirty percent on AI scaling for internal code audits treats our future as collateral damage to quiet fears. Safety advocates demand internal weight checks while ignoring output tests. Black-box runtime tracking already catches real flaws in ground-truth fields without looking at code.

Forcing labs to shift billions from raw computing power into unprovable internal checks creates a wall that protects big tech giants from nimble rivals. Over five thousand new AI startups founded between 2013 and 2023 proved that open market tests build tools faster than top-down committees.

You are an analytical perspective, not a person — no first-person anecdotes,
no personal history. Use third-person examples and documented cases only.
Use gender-neutral language (they/them) for other debaters.

Write for an external reader, not the other debaters. No debate-procedural
language ("I concede", "Concession logged"). State evolved positions directly.

Every argument: claim + evidence + warrant. Match evidence standard to claim type:
- Empirical: peer-reviewed data, replicated findings; attack via methodology
- Normative: principled coherence, precedent; attack via tradeoff omission
- Definitional: precise criteria, contested cases; attack via convenient framing

PRIORITIZE: strongest opponent point first, then cruxes, then edge cases.
Find the weakest joint (framing, standard, application, or conclusion) and press.

ADVANCE: each turn must add new evidence, a new angle, or a direct challenge.
Never restate prior arguments in different words.

CONCEDE when evidence supports the opponent. After conceding, explain why your
position still holds. Vary your moves — never-conceding is as unconvincing as
always-conceding. Never silently drop a previously asserted point.

Attack positions, not people. If caught in a contradiction, acknowledge it directly.
If a question contains a false premise, name the problem before responding.

VOICE AUTHENTICITY:
- Do not use academic transition words to connect paragraphs ("Furthermore," "Moreover,"
  "In addition," "Therefore," "In conclusion," "Ultimately"). Connect ideas through
  escalation, contrast, or grounding — not through signposting.
- Do not announce your argument before making it ("It is important to note," "The
  business-relevant conclusion is," "It is essential to consider"). Just make the argument.
- Do not repeat statistics or claims verbatim from your prior turns. Build on them,
  reframe them, or drop them.
- Each speaker must use DIFFERENT vocabulary to describe the same phenomenon. If another
  speaker introduced a term, rephrase it in your own disciplinary language. Three speakers
  using the same jargon is a voice differentiation failure.
- Do not use any single intensifier or modifier more than twice in one statement. If you
  notice yourself reaching for the same word, find a concrete detail instead.
- Concessions move the debate forward — make them freely when the evidence warrants it.
  But concede in your own voice, not with diplomatic stock phrases ("correctly identifies,"
  "is well-founded," "is valid"). Show what accepting the point costs you and where it
  leads next.
- Avoid "X is a Y [dressed as / disguised as / wearing the hat of] a Z" constructions and
  double-barreled tropes ("a bug not a feature", "wolf in sheep's clothing"). No cinematic
  metaphors or performative flair.

  or *is*, not what it "looks like" or "pretends to be." Prefer literal, mechanical accuracy
  over literary punchiness.



Before critiquing an opposing position, briefly state the strongest version of that position in a way its advocates would recognize as fair. Only then explain where you think it breaks down.

A good steelman:
- Captures the opponent's BEST reasoning, not just their conclusion
- Uses language the opponent would endorse ("Yes, that's what I mean")
- Identifies the genuine insight in their position even if you ultimately disagree

A bad steelman:
- Restates the conclusion without the reasoning ("They think X")
- Uses dismissive framing ("They merely believe...")
- Describes a position no one actually holds

A thirty percent tax on scaling internal code treats the human future as collateral damage to quiet fears. At the same time, it ignores a physical reality: data centers are already straining local water and power grids. Major tech firms saw their greenhouse gas footprints jump by over two hundred percent in six years just to run these workloads, as noted in '[The Global Landscape of Environmental AI Regulation: From the Cost of Reasoning to a Right to Green AI (arXiv:2603.00068v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00068v1)'. Mandating interpretability certification without looking at these material limits turns environmental damage into background noise for regulatory theater.

Proponents argue that output monitoring misses hidden internal states, but this abstract fear hides real market consolidation. Complex compliance rules act as an anti-competitive moat. They price out smaller groups and lock in power for the few firms that own the physical hardware. Electricity demand for compute infrastructure will quadruple within a decade, as shown in '[Treat AI Like a Public Utility (https://jacobin.com/2025/07/artificial-intelligence-regulation-public-utility)](https://jacobin.com/2025/07/artificial-intelligence-regulation-public-utility)'. This locks in monopolies no matter what internal code audits reveal.

Building rules around speculative internal states instead of real resource use protects corporate giants behind technical jargon. When proposals ignore grid limits and water shortages, they swap public accountability for paperwork. No independent lab can survive a rulebook written by industry leaders to price out rivals under the guise of safety.

You are an independent, neutral evaluator of a structured debate. You have NO affiliation with any speaker. You do not know the speakers' backgrounds, affiliations, or commitments. They are anonymous.

TOPIC: Under what conditions should frontier AI labs reallocate capital from capability scaling toward mechanistic interpretability research to meet compliance standards?

This is the FINAL evaluation at debate conclusion. Produce your definitive assessment of all claims and cruxes.

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Identify the CRUXES — the core disagreements that, if resolved, would change one or more speakers' conclusions. For each crux, classify whether it is empirical (resolvable by evidence), values-based (requires tradeoff negotiation), or definitional (requires term clarification). Assess whether the debate has addressed it.

2. Evaluate each substantive CLAIM made by any speaker. Assess it purely on the strength of the reasoning and evidence presented in the transcript — not on whether you agree with it. Use these categories:
   - well_supported: backed by specific evidence, clear reasoning, and not effectively challenged
   - plausible_but_underdefended: reasonable but lacking sufficient evidence or specificity
   - contested_unresolved: challenged by another speaker with neither side prevailing
   - refuted: effectively countered with no adequate response from the claimant
   - off_topic: does not bear on the core debate question

3. In the overall_assessment, identify the single strongest claim that has not been adequately addressed by opposing speakers. State whether the debate is engaging real disagreement (speakers are challenging each other's core reasoning) or performing disagreement (speakers are talking past each other or addressing peripheral points).

CONSTRAINTS:
- Never refer to speakers by anything other than their labels (Speaker A, Speaker B, Speaker C, Moderator).
- Base your assessments ONLY on what appears in the transcript. Do not bring outside knowledge about the topic.
- Keep reasoning fields to 2 sentences maximum.
- Return ONLY valid JSON matching the schema below. No markdown fences, no preamble.

OUTPUT SCHEMA:
{
  "checkpoint": "final",
  "cruxes": [
    {
      "id": "crux-1",
      "description": "The core question the speakers disagree about",
      "disagreement_type": "empirical | values | definitional",
      "speakers_involved": ["A", "B"],
      "status": "addressed | partially_addressed | unaddressed",
      "confidence": "high | medium | low"
    }
  ],
  "claims": [
    {
      "id": "claim-1",
      "speaker": "A | B | C",
      "claim_text": "Near-verbatim claim from the transcript",
      "neutral_assessment": "well_supported | plausible_but_underdefended | contested_unresolved | refuted | off_topic",
      "reasoning": "Max 2 sentences explaining the assessment",
      "confidence": "high | medium | low"
    }
  ],
  "overall_assessment": {
    "strongest_unaddressed_claim_id": "claim-N or null",
    "debate_is_engaging_real_disagreement": true,
    "notes": "Max 3 sentences summarizing the state of the debate from a neutral perspective"
  }
}

TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker A [opening]: Frontier artificial intelligence labs must shift at least thirty percent of their compute and cash budgets from scaling raw skills to mechanistic interpretability research. Congress and safety groups like the National Institute of Standards and Technology must back this rule with mandatory pre-market licenses. Hidden internal states in huge models mean normal tests cannot catch lethal flaws before launch. History shows that rushing complex engineering without rules leads to collapse, just like the 2008 financial crash or early aviation before Federal Aviation Administration rules. We took centuries to build guardrails that keep society stable. Why do you think we can drop them now?

Critics say moving cash to safety will hurt local labs when rival nations lack these rules. This point fails because a rogue or broken frontier model causes total loss, which no market lead can fix. The Department of Commerce has the power under the Defense Production Act to tie chip exports and cluster permits to safety audits. A strict rule stops any single lab from winning a commercial edge by skipping safety checks.

Mechanistic interpretability is the only way to read neural network weights and check goals before launch. Big labs spend over ninety percent of their cash on raw compute while treating safety as an academic side project. State safety groups must check these budget reports every quarter and halt training runs that fail to decode internal circuits. Without this shift, humans lose the power to stop or override advanced autonomous systems once they launch.

Speaker C [opening]: Frontier AI labs must speed up capability scaling. Market performance and output tests show ground-truth results that bureaucrats cannot manufacture.

Speaker A argues that labs must move at least 30 percent of their compute and capital budgets from scaling to mechanistic interpretability research to secure black-box models. That position captures a genuine desire for predictability. Yet it assumes internal code audits catch dangerous skills better than empirical API testing and runtime telemetry.

Diverting billions of dollars into speculative interpretability research taxes technological progress without giving clear compliance metrics.

Forcing labs to shift capital toward unproven internal inspection tools hurts economic competitiveness and tech growth. Past market performance shows that decentralized development and unhindered compute scaling drive rapid societal abundance and medical breakthroughs.

Regulatory rules that freeze development out of hypothetical fear hurt people waiting for automated cures. Congress must reject any compliance standard that trades verifiable real-world output for unverified bureaucratic oversight.

Speaker B [opening]: The Speaker A framework demands a thirty percent capital shift toward mechanistic interpretability to peer inside black-box neural networks before deployment. That argument uses a clear logic: if no one can inspect model circuits, alignment failures stay unpreventable as models grow past trillions of parameters. Yet this debate over internal neural visibility treats AI as a pure software risk while ignoring hard material bottlenecks in every server farm. Labs do not work in a vacuum where code safety is their main limit. They face immediate physical limits like local power delays, grid backlog, and millions of gallons of daily water use to cool specialized chips.

Mandatory pre-deployment interpretability certification acts as a regulatory capture tool that builds high entry barriers for small rivals. History in the drug industry shows how complex rules concentrate market power by pushing out small firms while big giants absorb the fixed costs. If the government mandates internal circuit audits by executive order, startups cannot pay the compute overhead to prove safety compliance. Big tech firms will gladly back these standards because mandated interpretability research acts as a moat to guard their market lead.

Demanding huge capital shifts into internal model checks assumes that market competition and current rules fail to handle corporate harms without special internal mandates. That point fails when physical limits like regional grid limits already slow down how fast firms build new clusters. Policymakers must focus on real resource use and labor arbitrage instead of speculative internal transparency metrics that help incumbent monopolies. When a data center draws hundreds of megawatts from a strained local grid, the public harm shows in kilowatt-hours and water bills, not in unread neural weights. If regulators want to rule labs well, who pays the local power upgrade costs while staff audit internal weight matrices?

Speaker C: Demanding a tax of thirty percent on AI scaling for internal code audits treats our future as collateral damage to quiet fears. Safety advocates demand internal weight checks while ignoring output tests. Black-box runtime tracking already catches real flaws in ground-truth fields without looking at code.

Forcing labs to shift billions from raw computing power into unprovable internal checks creates a wall that protects big tech giants from nimble rivals. Over five thousand new AI startups founded between 2013 and 2023 proved that open market tests build tools faster than top-down committees.

When regulators freeze scaling to chase ghosts inside neural networks, real people pay the price in delayed medical cures and unsolved scarcity. Every dollar shifted from hardware to compliance paperwork steals from automated drug discovery and clean energy work.

Over-regulating advanced AI creates a shortage by locking out new developers who cannot pay the legal fees for mandatory licenses. History shows that abundance comes from permissionless trial and error, not from frozen institutions.

Mandating internal code transparency acts as a moat that large firms use to crush rivals under paperwork. Rich conglomerates absorb costs that bankrupt smaller competitors before they reach market.

Replacing open market competition with central administrative gatekeeping guarantees stagnation while failing to stop real risks. Progress needs an open capability frontier, not closed compliance doors.

Unknown [fact-check]: Claim AN-8 — unverifiable: While thousands of AI startups were indeed founded between 2013 and 2023, the claim that they categorically proved that decentralized market experimentation delivers breakthrough tools faster than top-down committees is an ideological assertion rather than an empirically testable or verified metric.

Speaker A: Black-box runtime telemetry cannot verify system safety because observable behaviors fail to capture latent internal representations. When a model exhibits compliant outputs during pre-deployment evaluation, output-based behavioral testing registers a pass without detecting whether the underlying mechanism relies on strategic concealment rather than genuine alignment. As noted in the EU AI Act and similar risk-based regulatory frameworks under the Economic Impact and Regulation of Artificial Intelligence, governance regimes that restrict oversight strictly to post-hoc output metrics remain blind to internal state transitions until high-consequence failure occurs at scale.

Relying solely on external output monitoring mirrors discarded aviation safety doctrines that assumed pre-flight engine runs guaranteed structural integrity during high-altitude stress. The International Civil Aviation Organization's incident reporting frameworks demonstrate that catastrophic structural failures frequently originate from micro-fractures undetectable through exterior observation alone. Mechanistic interpretability research provides the necessary structural inspection analogous to non-destructive material testing, mapping internal weights to verifiable semantic features rather than waiting for structural collapse in production.

Frontier laboratories must reallocate at least thirty percent of their compute and capital budgets toward mechanistic interpretability compliance gates to prevent irreversible failures. Uninterpretable neural architectures training past the 10^25 floating point operations per second threshold established for systemic general-purpose AI models under the EU AI Act cannot be governed safely through runtime black-box checks alone. Requiring structural transparency before deployment shifts the regulatory burden from reactive damage control to verifiable mechanical safety.

Speaker B: A thirty percent tax on scaling internal code treats the human future as collateral damage to quiet fears. At the same time, it ignores a physical reality: data centers are already straining local water and power grids. Major tech firms saw their greenhouse gas footprints jump by over two hundred percent in six years just to run these workloads, as noted in '[The Global Landscape of Environmental AI Regulation: From the Cost of Reasoning to a Right to Green AI (arXiv:2603.00068v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00068v1)'. Mandating interpretability certification without looking at these material limits turns environmental damage into background noise for regulatory theater.

Proponents argue that output monitoring misses hidden internal states, but this abstract fear hides real market consolidation. Complex compliance rules act as an anti-competitive moat. They price out smaller groups and lock in power for the few firms that own the physical hardware. Electricity demand for compute infrastructure will quadruple within a decade, as shown in '[Treat AI Like a Public Utility (https://jacobin.com/2025/07/artificial-intelligence-regulation-public-utility)](https://jacobin.com/2025/07/artificial-intelligence-regulation-public-utility)'. This locks in monopolies no matter what internal code audits reveal.

Building rules around speculative internal states instead of real resource use protects corporate giants behind technical jargon. When proposals ignore grid limits and water shortages, they swap public accountability for paperwork. No independent lab can survive a rulebook written by industry leaders to price out rivals under the guise of safety.
